name: Uruguay
summary_text: Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected. The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality. For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and Montevideo is welcoming.

sources.title: Uruguay | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): broad protections - same-sex marriage since 2013, adoption since 2009, accessible legal gender recognition; since 2021 more than 120 trans people have accessed a reparation pension for institutional violence suffered during the 1973-1985 dictatorship; anti-discrimination law explicitly covers SOGI and hate-crime laws include SOGI aggravating circumstances.

sources.title: Ley N° 19684 Comprehensive Law for Trans People | Legal Information Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cornell Law School resource on Uruguay's Ley N° 19684 (2018), the Comprehensive Law for Trans People: ensures the right to a life free of discrimination and stigmatisation; the right to free development of personality per one's gender identity regardless of biological/genetic/anatomical factors; right to identification matching gender identity; includes reparation mechanisms.

sources.title: LGBT Rights in Montevideo, Uruguay | Equaldex
sources.claim_summary: Equaldex data for Montevideo (governed by federal Uruguay law): homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, gender-affirming care legal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected.

sources.title: Poder Ejecutivo promulgó ley integral para personas trans | Presidencia Uruguay
sources.claim_summary: Uruguayan Presidency (Nov 2018, in Spanish): the Executive promulgated the Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons (Law 19,684) - the right to gender identity and a life free of discrimination, name/sex change on identity documents, and a reparation regime for trans people born before 31 December 1975 who suffered institutional violence or deprivation of liberty.

sources.title: Uruguay: Freedom in the World 2024 Country Report | Freedom House
sources.claim_summary: Freedom House 2024 for Uruguay: 'Free' (96/100) - historically strong democratic governance; disparities remain in treatment and political representation of women, transgender people, Afro-Uruguayans and the Indigenous population.

sources.title: Remembering Our Dead - Joana (28 Jul 2025)
sources.claim_summary: Trans Lives Matter / TDoR memorial entry (July 2025): Joana, 29, a trans woman shot in the head at her home in Montevideo's Bella Italia neighbourhood; police hypothesised the attack targeted the man with her and she was a collateral victim; the perpetrator was sentenced to 7 years; the state expressed sorrow.

sources.title: Usuaria trans denunció maltrato y discriminación en el hospital de San Carlos | la diaria | Uruguay
sources.claim_summary: la diaria (May 2024, in Spanish): a trans user denounced mistreatment and discrimination at the San Carlos hospital - Andrea Gianneo, previously brutally beaten by a driver in Piriápolis (prompting a Piria Pride mobilisation), discussed the case with the health-centre director alongside a criminal complaint.

sources.title: Mujer trans en juicio contra BROU por discriminación denuncia ocultamiento de evidencia | Montevideo Portal
sources.claim_summary: Montevideo Portal (Sept 2025, in Spanish): a trans woman in a discrimination lawsuit against state bank BROU denounces concealment of evidence - Beccah Rivas says the bank did not deliver the main record requested by the prosecutor and that she lost her job after publicising the case.

sources.title: Uruguay's President grants legal rights for gay couples | PinkNews
sources.claim_summary: PinkNews (Dec 2007): Uruguay became the first Latin American country to recognise same-sex civil unions - President Tabare Vazquez signed the law granting cohabiting couples (5+ years) the same rights as married couples, 'of any sex, identity, orientation or sexual option'; the Episcopal Conference of Uruguay attacked the validity of gay relationships.
